q: The volume of an aluminium object is $40\,\text{cm}^3$ and its mass is $108\,\text{g}$. What is the density of aluminium in $\text{g/cm}^3$?
The volume of a cube doubles, but the substance stays the same. What happens to the mass and the density of the cube?
a: The mass doubles, because mass is directly proportional to volume, $m = \rho V$. The density does not change, because it is a property of the substance and the ratio $m : V$ stays the same.

q: The volume of a water bottle is $1.5\,\text{dm}^3$. What is the mass of the water ($\rho = 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$)? Which conversion is needed?
a: The volume is converted to cubic metres: $1.5\,\text{dm}^3 = 1.5 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$. Then $m = \rho V = 1000\,\tfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3} \cdot 1.5 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3 = 1.5\,\text{kg}$.
